..(Monday night through Saturday)
Issued at 435 AM EDT SUN OCT 11 2026

The extended portion of the forecast seems reasonable with focus
on the Southeast 5h ridge retreating out of Kentucky by mid week.
This should allow a frontal system to start to impact the state
from the north. Late in the week there looks to be a potential for
a stronger frontal passage in connection with a strong upper 
trough working into the Ohio Valley - though the models are not 
well aligned with this feature, at this point, reducing 
confidence in the specifics and timing details of this upcoming 
pattern change.

The previous long term discussion follows:

The extended period opens Monday morning with the remnant low 
from Isaias departing the area towards the northeast into the 
coastal Mid-Atlantic and Southern New England. A few residual 
light showers across the far eastern fringes of the Jackson CWA 
early Monday morning gives way to a strong upper-level ridge. An 
unseasonably warm and dry start to the extended forecast period 
across eastern Kentucky will yield to an active weather pattern by
mid-week, marked by a strong cold front, rising precipitation 
chances, and a sharp autumn cool- down for the weekend.

The strong upper-level ridge centered across the Central US and 
Ohio Valley, keeps eastern Kentucky under subsidence with 
decreasing clouds through the day. 500 mb heights running in the 
80th to 95th percentile for mid-October will push daytime 
temperatures well above seasonal normals through Thursday, 
generally ranging 5 to 10 degrees above normal in the upper 70s to
low 80s. Tuesdays forecast high temperature of 82 at the JKL 
airport is within 2 degrees of the established record high of 84, 
set back in 1985. In fact, the 00Z LREF ensemble shows a 35 to 40 
percent chance of reaching 84 degrees.

Model soundings from Monday and Tuesday afternoons show steep
low-level lapse rates from the surface to 850 mb with a
pronounced dry layer above the boundary layer. To account for
this boundary layer mixing, raw model guidance was blended with
the deterministic NBM to slightly lower dew points both
afternoons. Through the day Tuesday, the pressure gradient
across the area increases ahead of an approaching system from
the Central Plains. This increased gradient could lead to breezy
conditions in the Bluegrass and areas along and west of I-75
Tuesday afternoon, where wind gusts of 15 to 20 mph are
possible. While warm, dry, and a little breezy, fire weather
should not be of too much concern as min RH remains in the
upper 30s to mid 40s through the day.

High pressure anchored off the Southeast coast will maintain warm
advection through mid-week. However, a weak surface boundary
sagging south across the Ohio Valley will bring low-end rain
chances to eastern Kentucky Wednesday afternoon and evening.

A more significant pattern shift occurs Thursday as a cut-off
low over the Four Corners ejects northeastward toward the
Northern Plains and Upper Midwest. As the boundary lifts back
north as a warm front, a strengthening southerly low-level jet
will tap directly into Gulf moisture, advecting some across the 
Commonwealth. Model and ensemble agreement begins to drop toward 
the second half of the extended period. It will be interesting to 
see how this cutoff low from the Four Corners interacts with the 
northern stream as it approaches the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes
Thursday onward. Due to the uncertainty, the NBM deterministic 
has maintained smoothed-out isolated to scattered PoPs across the 
area Thursday and Friday. Some ensembles are showing PWATs across 
eastern Kentucky climbing from around 1.0 inch early Thursday to 
1.4 inches by Thursday evening and Friday morning - representing 
an anomalous moisture plume near the 90th percentile for mid- 
October. While the present forecast doesn't have heavy rainfall 
due to model uncertainty, the anomalous moisture plume in some 
ensembles hints that heavy rainfall near the end of the week 
remains a possibility.

A cold front associated with this late-week system could pass
through eastern Kentucky during the day Friday. Behind the front,
cold, dry continental polar air is modeled to intrude into the
Ohio Valley Friday evening and Saturday. PWAT steadily falls
through Saturday, modeled by some as low as 0.2 to 0.4 inches.
Temperatures that were once 5 to 10 degrees above normal could
swing 5 to 10 degrees below normal by next Saturday.
